items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Governance section: "Creating an AI systems inventory"
items.quote: A live inventory will help your team, your organisation and your stakeholders understand the scope and scale of AI usage.
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. Departments 'should set up' an inventory of AI and machine learning systems, in addition to their public transparency records, kept up to date with each system's purpose, usage, risks, data, ownership and key dates. Public sector guidance; no equivalent instruction exists for companies.

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: guidance for public sector bodies
items.locator: Section 2 (ATRS purpose and scope); section 2.1.4 (third party involvement)
items.quote: It is mandatory for all government departments, and for ALBs which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public.
items.why: The one UK register requirement that names algorithmic tools. In scope: tools with a significant influence on a decision with public effect, or which interact directly with the public. Records include fields for third-party suppliers, which is how procured tools are captured. A requirement of government policy, not statute; it does not reach the private sector.

items.title: Use of artificial intelligence in government (HC 612)
items.quote: Eight of 32 organisations responding to our survey that had deployed AI said they were always or usually compliant with the standard
items.why: Source of the figure. Survey of 87 government bodies in autumn 2023; the standard was 'not widely used'. The finding pre-dates the mandatory requirement announced in February 2024, so it measures a voluntary standard. Para 1.10 adds that 'a lack of central visibility of AI use may increase the risk of incomplete assurance'.

items.title: Supervisory Statement SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority
items.locator: Principle 1.2 (Model inventory), points (a)-(c), PDF p.11-12; para 1.3, PDF p.3
items.quote: A comprehensive model inventory should be maintained to enable firms to: identify the sources of model risk
items.why: The firmest UK regulatory expectation of an inventory. Covers models in use, in development and decommissioned, 'developed in-house or externally, including vendor models', held firm-wide, with purpose, assumptions, limitations and validation findings recorded. Applies only to banks, building societies and designated investment firms with internal model approval.

items.title: AI Management Essentials tool (consultation version, accessible)
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: We maintain a complete and up-to-date record of all the AI systems our organisation develops and uses.
items.why: Government's draft self-assessment for businesses puts the record first. It asks what proportion of systems are documented, whether there is a process for adding new ones, whether documentation is obtained from third-party providers, and how often the record is reviewed. Consultation version (closed 29 January 2025); voluntary.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle 5 (Identify, track and protect your assets), provision 5.1
items.quote: shall maintain a comprehensive inventory of their assets (including their interdependencies/connectivity)
items.why: A voluntary government code addressed to developers, system operators and data custodians. The inventory here is of assets, for security purposes, which is narrower than a governance register but rests on the same point: what is not listed cannot be protected.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities.
items.why: International comparator, and the plainest statement of the control. MAP 4.1 and 4.2, read alongside, ask for the risks of third-party software and data to be mapped and documented. Voluntary United States framework.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 49: Registration
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: shall register themselves, select the system and register its use in the EU database referred to in Article 71
items.why: EU comparator, and a caution. Registration under the AI Act is in a public EU database, by providers of listed high-risk systems and by public-authority deployers; it is not a duty on a private deployer to keep an internal register. Read on the European Commission's own copy, based on the consolidated text of 27 July 2026, because EUR-Lex returned an empty page. The brief makes no EU claim.

items.title: FS2/23: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (feedback statement)
items.publisher: Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority
items.quote: firms should maintain an inventory of high-risk AI use cases
items.why: Shows the idea of an AI-specific inventory reaching the financial regulators from industry. This was the view of one respondent to DP5/22, not a regulatory position; the statement contains no policy proposals.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 30: Records of processing activities
items.quote: Each controller and, where applicable, the controller's representative, shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility.
items.why: The nearest binding UK duty to a register: an organisation must keep a written record of its processing of personal data, with purposes, categories of data and recipients, and show it to the regulator on request. An AI system that handles personal data should already appear there. It covers personal data processing, not AI systems as such, and Art. 30(5) exempts organisations with fewer than 250 staff unless the processing is risky, not occasional, or involves special category data. Revised text as shown on the day read.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Accountability toolkit: Records of processing and lawful basis
items.locator: Second control measure (record of processing activities), with its 'Ways to meet our expectations'; first control measure on data mapping
items.quote: There is a formal, documented, comprehensive and accurate record of all processing activities (ROPA) based on a data mapping exercise that is reviewed regularly.
items.why: How the regulator audits a record of this kind: built from a mapping exercise, not from memory; kept electronically; reviewed against what people actually do; with named responsibility for keeping it current. The same tests separate a live AI register from a snapshot. Carries the 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025; the page shows no publication date, so the year is the year read. Data protection only, not AI governance in general.

items.title: ETSI EN 304 223 V2.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
items.locator: Clause 5.2.1, Principle 5 (Identify, track and protect the assets), Provisions 5.2.1-1 and 5.2.1-2, p.12
items.quote: shall have processes and tools to track, authenticate, manage version control and secure their assets
items.why: The free European Standard, adopted 8 December 2025, that carries the asset-inventory requirement of the UK's voluntary code into a formal standard (its history table shows it began as ETSI TS 104 223 in April 2025). It requires a comprehensive inventory of AI assets and the means to track them. A cyber security standard: 'assets' means models, data and related components, which is narrower than a register of AI uses with owner and risk tier. Voluntary unless adopted by contract or regulation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, NIST AI 600-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Suggested actions GV-1.6-001 to GV-1.6-003 (under GOVERN 1.6), printed p.16 (PDF p.20)
items.quote: Enumerate organizational GAI systems for incorporation into AI system inventory and adjust AI system inventory requirements to account for GAI risks.
items.why: A free standard, dated 2024, that extends the framework's inventory outcome to generative AI. Its next action tells organisations to decide in policy how generative AI built into other software is treated in the inventory, which is the 'embedded systems' part of this criterion. Voluntary, US, and limited to generative AI.

items.title: M-25-21: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust
items.publisher: Executive Office of the President, Office of Management and Budget (United States)
items.locator: Appendix, section 3(b)(v) 'Update AI Use Case Inventories', PDF p.12; Chief AI Officer duty to maintain the inventory, PDF p.11
items.quote: Each agency (except for the Department of Defense and the Intelligence Community) must inventory its AI use cases at least annually
items.why: International comparator: US federal agencies must list their AI use cases at least once a year, send the list to the budget office and publish a version, with a named Chief AI Officer responsible for keeping it. A firmer and more regular duty than the UK's publication standard. A binding instruction to US federal agencies only, not law for businesses, and non-UK. The PDF is a scanned copy with machine-read text.

items.title: Operationalising AI governance through ethics-based auditing: An industry case study
items.publisher: Jakob Mökander and Luciano Floridi (arXiv; published in AI and Ethics)
items.locator: Section 6.2 (Demarcating the material scope for AI governance), PDF p.14-15
items.quote: Without such an inventory, AI auditors depended on the business to identify and select relevant projects and systems for the in-depth audits.
items.why: A twelve-month case study of an AI audit at AstraZeneca. Without an agreed definition of what counted as AI the company could not assemble an inventory of its systems, so the auditors had to rely on the business to nominate what was examined. Direct evidence of what an incomplete register costs. Authors' arXiv preprint (posted 7 July 2024) of an article published in AI and Ethics in 2022 (doi 10.1007/s43681-022-00171-7); the journal copy could not be read. One company, one audit.

items.title: Dutch Comfort: The limits of AI governance through municipal registers
items.locator: Section on the registers' information voids, PDF p.10; see also p.4-5 and p.9
items.quote: the algorithmic register only reveals those systems that are housed by the municipality
items.why: A critical commentary on the public AI registers of Amsterdam and Helsinki: they listed a limited number of systems, left out the most harmful uses in welfare and policing, and missed systems run in the city by other bodies or third parties. A warning that a register can look complete and not be. Preprint as read (the arXiv page gives no journal reference); a commentary drawing on the authors' fieldwork, not a systematic study; about public registers in two cities, non-UK.
